data.text/markdown:
TimesFM 3.0, zero-shot: how well does a pre-trained model forecast stock prices?

TimesFM 3.0 is Google's pre-trained forecasting model (330 million parameters, released August 2026, shipped in Darts 0.48 as TimesFM3Model). It is used here zero-shot: it reads a stock's recent closes and forecasts the next bars without ever being trained or tuned on stocks. Every forecast comes as three paths: the median (half the outcomes above, half below) and a 10-90 % band that the price should stay inside 80 % of the time. Two questions, one section each:
  1. Intraday: from 1-minute bars, the next hour (never past the close)
  2. Multi-day: from 10-minute bars, the next five sessions (nights included)
Each section first shows single forecasts against the actual price, then grades every forecast in the window three ways:
  • path error: how far the median path is from the actual one, against the forecast "no change" (the price stays where it is). Prices are close to a random walk, so "no change" is the honest bar: a forecast that cannot beat it adds nothing.
  • direction: does the median end on the right side of the price when the forecast is made?
  • calibration: do the actual closes stay inside the 10-90 % band 80 % of the time?
Everything runs twice, on the price only and on the price + volume (volume as a past input, which TimesFM 3 can read beside the price). Beside every number sits a luck band: the same forecasts graded against the actual moves with their signs flipped at random (one coin per day, shared by every stock), which keeps each move's size and destroys any direction the model knows. A number inside its luck band is what a model without a clue gets.

Settings

The next cell holds every setting. Bars are counted in the section's own bar size: 1,170 one-minute bars are three sessions, 780 ten-minute bars are twenty.
  1. The stocks and the window: the five stocks of the direction study (liquid, very different movers), on the TUNE months only. The later months are locked in this folder (TEST, HOLDOUT): nothing here is trained, but what you see could still steer a choice.
  2. Intraday: the bar size, how many bars the model reads, how many it forecasts, and the clock times a forecast is made each day
  3. Multi-day: the same, one forecast after each session's close
  4. The run and the charts: the budget, the device, the luck-band draws and how much history the charts draw before each forecast

The data

The stored 1-minute bars of the regular session (09:30-16:00 New York), adjusted for dividends (a multi-day move across an ex-date would otherwise count the dividend as a loss). Each session is laid on a full clock grid: a minute without a stored bar takes the previous close and zero volume; half-days end at 13:00. The sessions are then joined end to end, so the model reads ONE series in which the next morning's first bar follows the close: the night's gap is a jump between two neighbouring bars. Every bar is stamped at its close time (the 1-minute bar from 09:59 to 10:00 is "10:00"), so a forecast "made at 10:00" reads the closes up to 10:00 and nothing later.

The model

  • Weights: google/timesfm-3.0-pytorch, snapshot 43046b85ec… (pinned: a new upload never changes a result silently). The first run downloads them (~1.3 GB) into the Hugging Face cache; later runs read them from there. They are under the TimesFM Non-Commercial License: fine for research and backtests, not for production trading.
  • Zero-shot: fit() only builds the network and loads the weights; nothing is trained.
  • One pass: each section has its own model, reading exactly the context and forecasting exactly the horizon in one pass, as Google's own code does (a longer output or a variable input length moves the paths by a few bp).
  • What it reads: the closes (price only), or the closes plus log(1 + volume) as a second series (price + volume). It scales every series itself, and if the context is close to a straight line (R² above about 0.75) it continues that line into the forecast: on a smooth trend it is a trend follower by design.
  • Output: the 10 %, 50 % and 90 % quantile of every future bar's close.
  • Speed and cache: about 35 ms a forecast on the Apple GPU (~3 minutes per section and setup at the defaults). Results are saved under var/timesfm_lab/, keyed by every setting and the exact numbers read; a rerun loads them in a second. Apple GPU and CPU agree to about 0.00002 dollars a share; the run is deterministic.

1 · Intraday: 1-minute bars, the next 60 minutes

Every session, at 10:00, 11:00, 12:00, 13:00, 14:00, 15:00, the model reads the last 1,170 bars (about 3.0 sessions: the earlier days' minutes, then today's so far) and forecasts the next 60. No forecast runs past the close: a half-day keeps only the forecasts that end by 13:00.

One forecast up close

Pick a stock, a day and a time. Figure 1 draws the actual price (black) before and after the forecast, the median path of each setup (blue: price only; green, dashed: price + volume), the price-only 10-90 % band (shaded) and the "no change" line (dotted). Below: the volume, dark up to the forecast, light after it (the model never sees the light part). The title gives this forecast's path error as a multiple of "no change" (below 1: better).

Every forecast of the section, graded. Path error saved: the share of the "no change" path error the median saves (0 % = no better, negative = worse). Direction right: the share of forecasts whose median ends on the right side of the starting price. End-move corr: how well the size and sign of the predicted end move line up with the actual one. Inside 10-90 % band: 80 % if the band is honest; below the 10 % line and above the 90 % line should each be 10 %. Says up / went up shows a lean: in a rising window a model that always says "up" is right more than half the time without knowing anything, and the luck band (signs flipped) does not catch that.

data.text/markdown:
2 · Multi-day: 10-minute bars, the next 5 sessions

After every session's close, the model reads the last 780 bars (about 20 sessions) and forecasts the next 195 (about 5 sessions, 39 bars each). The first forecast bar is the next morning's first 10 minutes, so the overnight gap is part of what it forecasts. Forecasts made on neighbouring days share most of their future, so the luck band flips one coin per 5 sessions.

Reading the results

  • Beating "no change" is the bar. A median path that wanders while the price wanders the other way costs more than the flat line. A positive path error saved, above its luck band, is the one sign the model knows where the price goes.
  • Direction and lean are different things. Compare "says up" with "went up": a model that continues the trend of a rising window says "up" more often and gets paid for the window, not for skill. The luck band keeps every move and flips its sign, so it removes the lean along with the direction.
  • A good band is still useful without direction. If the closes land inside the 10-90 % band about 80 % of the time, the model knows the SIZE of the coming moves (the earlier studies in this folder found size predictable and direction not), which is what risk limits, stops and position sizes need.
  • The settings are choices. Nothing is trained, but trying many contexts, horizons or clock times and keeping the best one is tuning: a best-of-many result needs a higher bar than one luck band, and the locked months as the final check.
